patient.chief_complaint: Rapid deterioration in gait and bladder control over 6 months — out of proportion to expected Alzheimer's progression
patient.history_present_illness: A 75-year-old retired architect was admitted for evaluation of rapid gait and bladder deterioration that his neurologist felt was disproportionate to his known Alzheimer's diagnosis. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease 14 months ago by a geriatric psychiatrist based on episodic memory impairment, normal structural MRI (at that time showing 'mild generalized atrophy'), and a clinical diagnosis. He was started on donepezil and memantine. Over the first six months his cognitive decline was gradual and he maintained mobility. However, in the past six months he has developed rapidly worsening gait — he now shuffles with extremely short steps and has had six falls. He needs a walker and cannot navigate stairs. Urinary incontinence began acutely four months ago, progressing rapidly to daily accidents. His wife states this is 'not like his Alzheimer's — something new is happening.' His cognitive decline also appears to have accelerated beyond the expected Alzheimer's trajectory. A repeat head MRI obtained last month showed 'enlarged ventricles' not present on the prior scan 14 months ago — Evans index now 0.37. His neurologist suspects superimposed NPH on Alzheimer's and has referred him for evaluation. The key clinical question is whether NPH is present and whether VP shunt would be beneficial given concurrent Alzheimer's diagnosis. The prior Alzheimer's diagnosis may or may not be fully accurate — CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET were not obtained at time of initial diagnosis.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person only. MoCA 16/30. Severe delayed recall (0/5), executive dysfunction, spatial disorientation. Moderate aphasia — anomia prominent. Reduced insight.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Full strength. No rigidity. No tremor.
neurological_exam.gait: Severely apraxic. Wide-based, very short shuffling steps. Freezing prominent. TUG 42 seconds with walker. Cannot do 10-meter walk test reliably due to freezing. Pull test — multiple steps, near fall.
neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Frontal release signs prominent. No nuchal rigidity.

signal_characteristics.description: Evans index 0.37 (new compared to 0.28 on prior MRI 14 months ago)
Moderate cortical atrophy, hippocampal atrophy disproportionate to frontal
Partially formed DESH — high-convexity effacement present but less florid

mri.impression: Interval development of ventriculomegaly (Evans index 0.37 compared to 0.28, 14 months ago) in a patient with known Alzheimer's disease and significant cortical atrophy. DESH pattern partially formed. Callosal angle 86° — borderline. The coexistence of significant cortical atrophy (AD) and new ventriculomegaly raises the possibility of NPH superimposed on Alzheimer's disease. This is a diagnostically challenging case. High-volume tap trial is reasonable but prognosis for shunt response is uncertain given AD copathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

special_tests.beta_amyloid_42: 448 pg/mL — LOW (diagnostic for Alzheimer's amyloid pathology)
special_tests.phospho_tau: 78 pg/mL — ELEVATED (consistent with AD tau pathology)

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 16 cmH2O. WBC: 2 cells/mcL (N/A PMN/N/A lymph). Protein: 52 mg/dL. Glucose: 68 mg/dL (ratio 0.72). cytology: No malignant cells. beta_amyloid_42: 448 pg/mL — LOW (diagnostic for Alzheimer's amyloid pathology). total_tau: 682 pg/mL — ELEVATED (consistent with neurodegeneration). phospho_tau: 78 pg/mL — ELEVATED (consistent with AD tau pathology). ptau_abeta_ratio: 0.174 — elevated, consistent with AD.

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (40 mL) with quantitative gait assessment

findings.cognitive: MoCA 16 to 17 at 24 hours (1 point — marginal)

specialized_test.impression: Borderline-negative single tap trial: 19% TUG improvement at 24 hours (threshold is 20%). Cognitive improvement marginal (1 MoCA point). This may represent: (1) false-negative tap trial (~40% false-negative rate), (2) dominant AD pathology limiting NPH shunt response, or (3) combined NPH-AD with partial tap response. Extended lumbar drainage trial (72h, 150-200 mL/day) is recommended before declaring tap-negative.
recommended_actions: Extended lumbar drainage trial — 72h at 150 mL/day
Amyloid PET for definitive AD quantification
Neurology-neurosurgery conference to weigh shunt risk-benefit in AD copathology

findings.result: Strongly positive amyloid PET — CL score 82

output.impression: Strongly positive amyloid PET (CL 82). Confirms concurrent Alzheimer's disease. NPH-AD copathology is confirmed. VP shunt may provide benefit for the NPH component (particularly gait) but cognitive improvement will be limited by underlying AD. Prognosis for cognitive recovery is poor; gait may partially improve.
recommended_actions: Multidisciplinary discussion about VP shunt risk-benefit ratio in NPH-AD copathology
Extended drainage trial before final shunt decision

output.test_type: Extended lumbar drainage (72h, 150 mL/day) — continuous external lumbar drain
output.impression: Extended drainage confirms NPH component: TUG improved 33% at 72h. Single tap trial was a false-negative. This patient has confirmed NPH superimposed on Alzheimer's disease. VP shunting is recommended for the NPH component. Cognitive benefit will be limited by concurrent AD, but gait and urinary control improvements are expected.
recommended_actions: VP shunt — programmable valve; patient and family counseled that cognitive improvement may be modest due to concurrent AD
Gait and urinary improvement are realistic goals

output.query: NPH Alzheimer copathology VP shunt outcomes positive amyloid PET

results.title: Shunt outcomes in NPH with concurrent Alzheimer's pathology — multicenter registry
results.key_finding: VP shunt in NPH-AD copathology improves gait in 60-70% and urinary symptoms in 50-60%; cognitive improvement is significantly reduced (20-30% vs 65% in pure NPH). Amyloid PET CL >50 associated with poor cognitive shunt response.

results.title: Extended drainage to predict shunt response in complex NPH
results.key_finding: Extended lumbar drainage (72h) identifies 35-40% additional responders missed by single tap trial; recommended when single tap is borderline-negative

output.summary: This patient has confirmed NPH-AD copathology (amyloid PET CL 82, CSF biomarkers diagnostic for AD). Extended drainage confirmed NPH component. VP shunt prognosis: gait improvement likely (60-70%); cognitive improvement limited by AD. Family must be counseled on realistic expectations — shunt will not reverse the Alzheimer's component.

output.impression: Some frontal-subcortical improvement with drainage (executive function, processing speed) but memory remains severely impaired — consistent with dominant AD-related episodic memory dysfunction that will not respond to shunting. VP shunt realistic for gait and urinary improvement, not memory recovery.

findings.result: Mildly reduced bilateral putaminal uptake — symmetric, mildly abnormal. Pattern not consistent with typical PD (asymmetric posterior putaminal loss).

output.impression: Mildly reduced symmetric putaminal uptake — may reflect AD-associated dopaminergic changes or DLB. Not typical of Parkinson's disease. Does not significantly change NPH-AD management but reduces likelihood of DLB as third comorbidity.
recommended_actions: Continue current management — DLB less likely given symmetric mild change
If DLB considered, trial cholinesterase inhibitor (already on donepezil)

output.query: NPH VP shunt decision making Alzheimer's disease copathology goals of care

results.title: Shared decision-making in NPH-AD copathology: a framework for neurologists and families
results.key_finding: Goals of care discussion essential before VP shunting in NPH-AD — focus on gait/fall prevention and quality of life, not cognitive recovery. Patient/family values must guide shunt decision when prognosis is uncertain.

output.summary: Shared decision-making with the patient (with wife's support given cognitive impairment) should focus on: (1) realistic goals — gait improvement and fall reduction, not cognitive recovery; (2) VP shunt risks (infection, subdural hematoma, over-drainage) vs benefits; (3) family caregiver burden from falls. Extended drainage confirmed NPH component — shunting is reasonable with appropriate goal-setting.

CSF biomarkers (amyloid-42 448, p-tau 78) and amyloid PET (CL 82) confirm concurrent Alzheimer's disease

critical_actions: Obtain CSF biomarkers at time of LP — critical for diagnosing AD copathology
Perform amyloid PET given borderline-positive tap and cognitive severity
Recognize that single tap borderline-negative does not exclude NPH — extended drainage is required
Counsel family that VP shunt will help gait and urinary symptoms, NOT cognitive decline from Alzheimer's

Proceeding to VP shunt without amyloid PET/CSF biomarkers to confirm AD copathology
Counseling family that VP shunt will reverse the Alzheimer's dementia

CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET confirmed concurrent Alzheimer's (not just clinical diagnosis from 14 months ago)

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Interval ventriculomegaly, extended drainage response, and clinical rate of decline suggest superimposed NPH. Concurrent diagnosis requires both conditions to be addressed.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Single tap has 35-40% false-negative rate. Extended drainage confirmed 33% TUG improvement at 72h — NPH component is real and treatable.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Interval ventriculomegaly (Evans 0.28→0.37), partial DESH, callosal angle 86°, and extended drainage response confirm true NPH physiology superimposed on AD-related atrophy.
